: Module overview {.striped}

The module is an elective in the handbooks of M.Sc. VWL and M.Sc. BWL (PNPM).

## Prerequisites

Mathematics, statistics, probability theory, and regression analysis (estimation
and hypothesis testing). Python is essential for the exercise sessions.

## Content

The module covers the fundamentals of Bayesian inference and their application to
high-dimensional datasets in economics and finance, with equal weight on
theoretical foundations and empirical implementation in Python.

- Subjective probability and the Bayesian paradigm
- MCMC algorithms: Gibbs sampling and Metropolis-Hastings
- Shrinkage and the Minnesota prior
- BVARs and state-space models for macroeconomics
- Stochastic volatility and portfolio choice
- Bayesian machine learning for causal inference

## Learning outcomes

After completing the module, students are able to

- explain the theoretical foundations of Bayesian inference and subjective probability,
- analyse complex, high-dimensional datasets with modern Bayesian techniques,
- apply Bayesian econometric methods to empirical problems in economics and finance,
- implement standard Bayesian algorithms and models in original Python code,
- critically evaluate empirical findings while accounting for uncertainty.

## Weekly plan {#weekly-plan}

::: {.callout-note}
### Dates
Exact dates and room assignments are confirmed on ILIAS before the term starts.
Each week pairs a 90-minute lecture (2 SWS) with an exercise session (2 SWS) in which the
week's method is implemented in Python.
:::

### Foundations

| Week | Lecture | Content | Literature | Exercise (Python) |
|:--|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Introduction: The Bayesian Paradigm | Subjective probabilities, Bayes' theorem, priors, likelihoods, and posteriors | Koop (2003); Zellner (1971) | Grid search: calculating a posterior for a beta-binomial model using discrete grids |
| 2 | The Linear Regression Model | Normal-Inverse-Gamma conjugate priors, analytical solutions, and marginal posterior distributions | Koop (2003); Box and Tiao (1973) | Matrix update: manual NIG update for CAPM betas using only algebra |
| 3 | Monte Carlo Integration and Importance Sampling | Random sampling for approximating integrals, numerical estimation of expected values, and importance weighting | Geweke (1989); Robert (2004) | Vanilla MC: coding an option pricing simulator that incorporates parameter uncertainty |

: {.striped}

### Computation

| Week | Lecture | Content | Literature | Exercise (Python) |
|:--|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | Gibbs Sampling | MCMC fundamentals, full conditional distributions, and iterative sampling mechanics | Casella (1992); Gelfand (1990) | The workhorse: programming a Gibbs sampler for multiple regression from scratch |
| 5 | Metropolis-Hastings and NUTS Sampling | Acceptance-rejection algorithms for non-conjugate models, proposal distributions, and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo | Chib (1995); Hoffman (2014) | HMC vs MH: comparing sampling efficiency for a non-conjugate logistic model |
| 6 | Minnesota Priors | Minnesota priors and the logic of regularization to prevent overfitting in large models | Banbura (2010); Rubio-Ramirez (2010) | Prior tuning: manual construction of the Minnesota covariance matrix for large systems |

: {.striped}

### Macro & Policy

| Week | Lecture | Content | Literature | Exercise (Python) |
|:--|---|---|---|---|
| 7 | BVARs and Identification | Multivariate systems and sign restrictions to identify structural shocks | Banbura (2010); Rubio-Ramirez (2010) | BVAR lab: estimating a 3-variable system with sign-restricted impulse responses |
| 8 | State Space and Time-Varying Parameter Models | The Kalman filter and drifting coefficients in time-varying parameter models | Primiceri (2005); Durbin and Koopman (2012) | TVP filter: coding the Kalman recursions to track drifting market betas over time |
| 9 | Prediction and Bayesian Model Averaging | Posterior predictive distributions and Bayesian model averaging for robust forecasts | Madigan and Raftery (1994) | Backtesting: calculating log-predictive scores and weighting models via BMA |
| 10 | Causal Inference | Bayesian IV and treatment effects using BART for policy analysis | Imbens and Rubin (2015); Hill (2011) | Policy impact: estimating causal effects with BART and quantifying the uncertainty |

: {.striped}

### Finance

| Week | Lecture | Content | Literature | Exercise (Python) |
|:--|---|---|---|---|
| 11 | Variable Selection and Big Data | Taming the quadrillion-regressions problem with sparsity versus shrinkage priors | Kozak (2020); Giannone et al. (2015) | SSVS sampler: coding a spike-and-slab algorithm to select relevant finance factors |
| 12 | Stochastic Volatility | Latent volatility processes and time-varying risk models | Kim et al. (1998); Jacquier (1994) | SV sampler: MCMC implementation for log-volatility using the JPR algorithm |
| 13 | Portfolio Choice | Expected utility and decision theory under parameter and model uncertainty | Avramov (2010) | Robust allocation: maximizing expected utility using MCMC predictive draws |
| 14 | Bayesian Machine Learning | Gaussian processes and probabilistic neural nets for non-linear finance | Chipman (2010); Rasmussen (2006) | Non-linear Bayes: comparing BART versus OLS for predicting returns with non-linearities |

: {.striped}

### Review

| Week | Lecture | Content | Literature | Exercise (Python) |
|:--|---|---|---|---|
| 15 | Q&A and Review | Review lectures and open questions |  | Review: troubleshooting student code |

: {.striped}

## Assessment {#assessment}

### Examination

The module is assessed by a **written final exam of 90 minutes**.

Permitted aids in the exam:

- a non-programmable calculator,
- a hard copy of a German–English dictionary (book form), and
- a one-sided A4 hand-written cheat sheet.

### Grading

The final grade is based **100% on the written exam**.

### How to prepare

The exam tests both the theory and your ability to reason about Bayesian methods,
not your ability to run code under time pressure. The most reliable preparation is
to work through every exercise yourself during the term rather than reading the
solutions. Use the one-page cheat sheet as a forcing function: condensing the
material onto a single side is itself a good revision exercise.

::: {.callout-note}
The examination requirements follow the examination regulations of your
programme. Consult your programme's examination regulations and module handbook
for the binding requirements. Exam announcements and news are posted on ILIAS.
:::

## Reading {#reading}

Koop’s *Bayesian Econometrics* provides a starting point for the course.
Each chapter has its own reading guide with the relevant textbook sections
and research papers; you do not need to read every book listed here.

### Introductory textbooks

- Chan, Joshua, et al. *Bayesian Econometric Methods*. Cambridge University Press, 2019.
- Gelman, Andrew, et al. *Bayesian Data Analysis*. Chapman and Hall/CRC, 2013.
- Geweke, John. *Contemporary Bayesian Econometrics and Statistics*. John Wiley & Sons, 2005.
- Koop, Gary M. *Bayesian Econometrics*. Wiley, 2003.
- Lambert, Ben. *A Student's Guide to Bayesian Statistics*. Sage Publishing, 2018.

### Further textbooks and monographs

- Box, George E. P., and George C. Tiao. *Bayesian Inference in Statistical Analysis*. Addison-Wesley, 1973.
- Durbin, James, and Siem Jan Koopman. *Time Series Analysis by State Space Methods*. 2nd ed. Oxford University Press, 2012.
- Imbens, Guido W., and Donald B. Rubin. *Causal Inference for Statistics, Social, and Biomedical Sciences*. Cambridge University Press, 2015.
- Rasmussen, Carl E., and Christopher K. I. Williams. *Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning*. MIT Press, 2006.
- Robert, Christian P., and George Casella. *Monte Carlo Statistical Methods*. 2nd ed. Springer, 2004.
- Zellner, Arnold. *An Introduction to Bayesian Inference in Econometrics*. Wiley, 1971.
